passage:
Thursday night. Asked Farida to swap Saturday's shift so I could go to my cousin's engagement. Farida said, "Sorry, can't." Asked two others. Same answer. Nobody even looked up. It stings. Three weeks ago I insisted the release schedule stay my way, with testing on Mondays. I brought numbers and made sure everyone knew I was right. I won. Nobody argued after that. Since then people hand me tasks on the shared board without a word and have stopped coming to my desk. Farida told me back then, "It only works for you." I said the numbers say otherwise. Tonight I think I won the argument and lost something else. Maybe I should ask what Monday testing costs them.

Sandeep

qa.q: What did Farida say when asked to swap the shift?

qa.a: Sandeep feels hurt and uneasy, saying that it stings and that something else was lost.

qa.q: What could Sandeep do to repair things with colleagues?
qa.a: Sandeep could ask colleagues what Monday testing costs them and look for a schedule that works for everyone.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen the original schedule fight?
qa.a: Farida may have felt unheard, having said it only worked for Sandeep, and later unwilling to do favours.

grounding: Shows a team member winning a schedule argument by insisting, then finding colleagues stop cooperating and refuse favours.

passage:
Office shift group, October

Gautam: I'm taking Diwali week off. Already told the manager.
Yash: Bro, we agreed to split it. I haven't been home since March.
Gautam: I asked first. Rules are rules.
Yash: Can we at least talk?
Gautam: Nothing to talk about. Done.

December

Gautam: Hey, can someone cover my Saturday? Family function 🙏
(no replies for two hours)
Gautam: Yash?
Yash: Can't.
Gautam: Anyone?
Yash: You said rules are rules.

Gautam put the phone down. Since Diwali, nobody had asked him to lunch. He had won the week off. He hadn't noticed what he'd lost.

qa.q: What did Gautam say when Yash asked to talk?
What does Yash's reply 'You said rules are rules' suggest about how Yash feels?
qa.a: Yash still feels hurt and resentful about Diwali, and throws Gautam's own words back at him.

qa.q: What could Gautam have done differently in October?
qa.a: He could have asked what mattered most to Yash, maybe splitting Diwali week, so both got some time home and the team stayed friendly.

qa.q: How do the other colleagues see Gautam after Diwali?
qa.a: They seem to have cooled on him; nobody replies for two hours and nobody asks him to lunch.

grounding: A team member insists on his schedule and wins, but colleagues stop cooperating and later refuse him a favour.

passage: At the small cooperative dairy outside Nashik, there was one delivery van for two routes. Eshaan wanted it every morning for the town route, where the big orders were. Sahil needed it on Tuesdays for the villages. At the monthly meeting, Eshaan argued loudly, listed his sales figures, and the secretary gave him the van every morning. Eshaan left smiling. But over the next weeks, Sahil stopped helping him load crates. The storeman became slow with Eshaan's slips. When the van broke down in November and Eshaan asked Sahil to lend his motorbike for one urgent drop, Sahil shook his head. "Ask the secretary," he said. Eshaan stood by the milk cans, realising the win had cost him every favour he used to get free.

qa.q: Which days did Sahil need the van?
What was Eshaan feeling as he stood by the milk cans?
qa.a: Eshaan felt stunned and regretful, realising his win had cost him the goodwill of the people around him.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were Eshaan?
qa.a: Apologise to Sahil and offer to give up the van on Tuesdays, rebuilding trust before asking for anything else.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Eshaan after the meeting?
qa.a: Sahil sees him as someone who takes everything, so he feels no pull to help when Eshaan is in trouble.

grounding: A team member wins the argument over the van, but colleagues stop cooperating and later refuse him a favour.
